clue.text: Cook's vessel taking river away from Northern town

indicators.note: taking, paired with away from, says one piece is subtracted from the town's name
away from names the town as the word the river abbreviation is removed from

parts.note: Stockport is a town in Greater Manchester, in the north of England

explanation.surface: A chef's pan is somehow linked to diverting a river from a town up north.
explanation.walkthrough: STOCKPORT is a town near Manchester in northern England; 'taking' ... 'away from' removes R (river) from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stockpot is a large deep pan in which a cook simmers stock, so it is a kitchen vessel.

clue.text: Wanton English author

definitions.meaning: a wanton, an old word for a promiscuous woman or slattern

explanation.definitionFit: The noun once meant a slovenly or immoral woman, and it is also the surname of the novelist Anthony Trollope.

clue.text: Competitor for professor of literature

definitions.meaning: a contender who issues a challenge to a champion
Professor ..., the irascible scientist in Conan Doyle's The Lost World

explanation.definitionFit: A contender for a title is a challenger, and Conan Doyle's fictional scientist hero is Professor Challenger.

clue.text: Cured ham-it's poor cut, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the preceding letters come out jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone laments that their expensive cured ham has been sliced badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges the ten letters of IT'S POOR CUT; the hyphen after 'ham' is just a dash in the original.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosciutto is the Italian dry-cured ham, usually served in thin slices.

clue.text: Wheel turned left to go around

indicators.note: to go around asks the letters to circulate into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A wheel was turned leftwards so that it would revolve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' looks like the anagram signal but is fodder: 'to go around' shuffles TURNED with L (left).
explanation.definitionFit: To trundle is to roll or wheel something heavy along, so wheel as a verb fits.

clue.text: I party over island

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the word is read upwards, so it comes out backwards

parts.note: Lab is the short form of the Labour Party

explanation.surface: Someone declares that, as far as they are concerned, the party is finished on the island.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour is one of Britain's main political parties; in a down clue 'over' means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Bali is an Indonesian island east of Java.

clue.text: Source of pictures occurred to artist

parts.note: came, as in 'it came to me', means occurred
RA, a Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist

explanation.surface: An idea for where pictures come from strikes a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of London's Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: A camera is the device that produces photographs, so it is literally where pictures come from.

clue.text: Court risk when going over railway

indicators.note: in a down clue going over places the first piece above, that is before, the second

parts.note: to chance something is to risk it

explanation.surface: Gambling on running across a railway line could land you in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Chancery is a division of the English High Court, historically the Lord Chancellor's court of equity.

clue.text: Once more assign right diplomat back to the front

indicators.note: the back letter of the diplomat word is shifted round to its front

parts.note: an attache is a junior diplomat at an embassy

explanation.surface: An official is posted again, with a diplomat brought back to the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back to the front' takes the diplomat's final letter round to the start, so the word's last E opens the answer after R.
explanation.definitionFit: To reattach someone is to attach, or assign, them again to a post or unit.

clue.text: Fruit — two tiny pieces side by side, trimmed on both edges

indicators.note: trimmed on both edges cuts away the very first and very last letters of the doubled run
two says the word for tiny pieces is written out twice in a row

parts.note: an atom is a tiny particle, the classic image of a minute piece

explanation.surface: Two tiny bits of fruit placed next to each other have been neatly trimmed at the ends.
explanation.walkthrough: ATOM twice gives ATOMATOM; 'trimmed on both edges' takes off the first A and the final M.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanically the tomato is a fruit, a berry of the nightshade family.

clue.text: South American wader nipped after my boy, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: my boy is SON and nipped is BITTEN, placed after it

explanation.surface: A wading bird bit somebody's son, or so the story goes.
explanation.walkthrough: SON followed by BITTEN, said in a non-rhotic British accent, sounds like the bird's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The sunbittern is a heron-like wading bird of tropical Central and South American rivers.

clue.text: How the author does without wife or domestic

indicators.note: without says the wife letter is dropped from what precedes

parts.note: taken as written
the author refers to the setter, who would say me

explanation.surface: A question about how a writer manages without a spouse or a housekeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the author' is the setter speaking of themself, ME; 'without' takes W (wife) from HOWME.
explanation.definitionFit: Home is an adjective meaning domestic, as in home affairs or the home market.

clue.text: Give example of prostitute held back by hard treatment

indicators.note: held by means the second piece sits inside the hard-treatment word

parts.note: ill-use means cruel or harsh treatment

indicators.note: back says the word for prostitute is read in reverse

parts.note: tart is slang for a prostitute

explanation.surface: A tale of a sex worker kept captive and roughly handled is offered as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: TART turned by 'back' gives TRAT, which ILL-USE holds: ILLUS-TRAT-E.
explanation.definitionFit: To illustrate a point is to give an example of it or show it by instance.

clue.text: Wartime ailment — suffering's hard in footwear

indicators.note: in tells us the suffering and hard pieces go inside the footwear word

parts.note: a sock is worn on the foot
hell is great suffering; with the 's it gives HELLS
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A soldier's war affliction is described as agony in his boots.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'suffering's' supplies a letter here, since it stands for 'is': HELLS plus H go inside SOCK.
explanation.definitionFit: Shell shock was the name for the psychological trauma suffered by soldiers in the First World War.

clue.text: Gooseberry's relative offering fiery tirade about scoundrel

indicators.note: about here means the tirade concerns the scoundrel, so it follows that word

parts.note: red describes the colour of fire
a cur is a contemptible man
a rant is an angry tirade

explanation.surface: A gooseberry's cousin is said to be delivering a furious outburst at a rogue.
explanation.definitionFit: The redcurrant and gooseberry are both shrubs of the genus Ribes, so they are botanical relatives.

clue.text: Engineers want island at start of street in Surrey town

indicators.note: at start of puts the engineers and island pieces in front of the street word

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers of the British Army
gate is an old northern word for a street, as in York's Stonegate

explanation.surface: Engineers want an island at the head of a street in a Surrey town.
explanation.walkthrough: GATE means street in northern English place names; REIGATE is a town in Surrey, a county south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Reigate is a market town in the county of Surrey, south of London.

clue.text: Call on party where people come close to fighting

definitions.text: where people come close to fighting

indicators.note: on, in a down clue, puts the first piece above, so before, the second

parts.note: to ring is to call on the telephone
a side is a party in a dispute or game

explanation.surface: Someone phones a party, and spectators press up close to a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: The ringside is the area beside a boxing ring where spectators sit nearest to the bout.

clue.text: God's eye roving and surveying the earth

indicators.note: roving suggests wandering about, so the letters move into a new order

parts.note: the letters of God's eye, with the S kept

explanation.surface: God's eye wanders across the planet, keeping watch.
explanation.definitionFit: Geodesy is the science of measuring the shape and size of the earth, so it is surveying on a global scale.

clue.text: Creator of incentives? Whacking rise draws in contented noises

indicators.note: draws in says the rearranged letters take the contented noises inside them
whacking implies battering, so the following word is knocked out of shape

parts.note: purr is the sound a contented cat makes

explanation.surface: A motivator asks whether a rise beaten up gathers contented murmurs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whacking' turns RISE into SIER, which 'draws in' PURR. The question mark marks a pun: a spurrier makes spurs, and a spur is also an incentive.
explanation.definitionFit: A spurrier is a maker of spurs, and a spur is an incentive, hence the punning question mark.

clue.text: Noisy celebration swinging bar mounted with turn of year

indicators.note: swinging means the bar is swung round, so its letters run the other way

parts.note: a lever is a bar used to prise or shift things

indicators.note: turn of says the abbreviation for year is turned back to front

explanation.surface: At a New Year party the drinkers swing from the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swinging' and 'turn of' both signal a reversal; 'mounted with' simply sets one piece on the other in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Revelry is lively, noisy festivity, the merrymaking at a celebration.

clue.text: Doreen turned out very lazy

indicators.note: turned out implies something has been turned inside out, so the name's letters are mixed

parts.note: well can mean very, as in well pleased

explanation.surface: It turned out that Doreen was really idle.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads Doreen as a person turning out lazy; 'turned out' is the anagram signal. The answer is usually a noun but works adjectivally.
explanation.definitionFit: Used adjectivally, ne'er-do-well describes a good-for-nothing, idle person.

clue.text: English fifty-one/nine up at rugby initially is a tonic

parts.note: LI is fifty-one in Roman numerals

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the numeral is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: IX is nine in Roman numerals

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A match report counts English players and a fifteen at rugby before offering a pick-me-up.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' turns IX into XI; 'initially' takes R from rugby.
explanation.definitionFit: An elixir is a supposedly restorative potion, so it is a tonic.

clue.text: Negative response of upper-class Henry finding university hard

parts.note: U is the label for upper-class usage
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A posh Henry says no on discovering that university is tough.
explanation.walkthrough: U as upper-class comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U, a famous essay on British class speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Uh-uh is the informal grunt people make to mean no.

clue.text: He left hobbits weird cultural custom

indicators.note: weird suggests something strange or odd, so the letters are arranged oddly

explanation.surface: Tolkien's little folk struck a visitor as having odd local habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weird' rearranges HE, L (left) and HOBBITS.
explanation.definitionFit: A shibboleth is a custom or usage that marks someone as belonging to a particular group.

clue.text: What goes under cakes shedding topping that's greasy

indicators.note: shedding topping removes the first letter, which in a down answer is at the top

parts.note: a doily is the lacy paper mat placed under cakes on a plate

explanation.surface: A lacy cake mat, minus its top layer, has gone greasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shedding topping' takes the D off DOILY; in a down clue the first letter is the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Oily means covered in or like oil, so greasy.

clue.text: Reversing America's cut in farm store plant

indicators.note: reversing means the assembled letters are read backwards
in says the American cutting tool goes inside the farm store

parts.note: a silo stores grain or fodder on a farm
ax is the American spelling of axe, a tool that cuts

explanation.surface: A tale of US spending cuts being reversed at a farm store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'America's cut' misleads as budget cuts: it is the US spelling of the tool. 'Reversing' applies to the whole assembled run.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxalis is a genus of plants, the wood sorrels, with clover-like leaves.

clue.text: One running at mouth — of goal?

definitions.text: One running at mouth — of goal?

parts.words: One running at mouth — of goal?
parts.note: one person running at the mouth drools; a footballer running with the ball at the goalmouth does the same in another sense

explanation.definitionFit: Someone who drools lets saliva run from the mouth, and a footballer who keeps the ball with small kicks does so near goal.

clue.text: Some buy a kit or instructions for exotic cookery

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Advice to purchase a kit or instruction booklet for cooking foreign dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Yakitori is Japanese grilled chicken on skewers, a dish exotic to Western cooks.
